title: Protective effects of Danzhi jiangtang capsule on vascular endothelial damages induced by high-fat diet and palmitic acid.

Protective eﬀects of Danzhi jiangtang capsule on vascular endothelial
damages induced by high-fat diet and palmitic acid
Yunxia Lua,b,⁎, Yong Chena,1, Rui Lic, Quan Liuc, Nuojin Wangd, Yi Zhangd, Bao Lib, Zhaohui Fange
a Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, Anhui Medical University, Hefei, Anhui 230032, PR China

A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords:
Danzhi jiangtang capsule
Oxidative stress
Endoplasmic reticulum stress
High-fat diet
Palmitic acid
Endothelial dysfunction
A B S T R A C T
Danzhi jiangtang capsule (DJC) is mainly used to treat type 2 diabetes mellitus and vascular complication. Our
aim was to investigate whether the protective eﬀects of DJC by oral administration on high-fat diet (HFD) and
palmitic acid-induced damages of endothelial cells are related to oxidative stress and endoplasmic reticulum
(ER) stress. Male Sprague-Dawley rats were randomly divided into standard chow diet (SCD), HFD, HFD plus
DJC-low dose (HFD + DJCL) and HFD plus DJC-high dose treatment groups (HFD + DJCH). The latter three
groups were given HFD feeding for three months, then the HFD + DJCL and HFD + DJCH rats were treated with
DJC (500 and 1000 mg/kg/day) via gavage for another two months respectively. Endothelium-dependent re-

in

Malondialdehyde (MDA), total-antioxidant capacity (T-AOC), superoxide dismutase (SOD), interleukin 1β (IL-
1β), tumour necrosis factor α (TNFα), free fatty acids (FFA), endothelin-1 (ET-1) and nitric oxide (NO) levels in
serum were assayed. The pathological changes, protein expression of endothelial NO synthase (eNOS), phos-
phorylated eNOS (p-eNOS) and ER stress-related genes in the thoracic aorta were measured. Human umbilical
vein endothelial cells (HUVEC) were treated with serum-medicated DJC and then with palmitic acid to detect the
reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels and C/EBP homologous protein (CHOP) distribution, expression of p-eNOS
and ER stress-related genes. DJC therapy exhibited a potent antioxidant activity and eﬀectively prevented the
endothelial dysfunction (ED) manifested by promoting p-eNOS expression and enhancing NO release, decreasing
lipid deposition (Oil-red O staining, CPT1b and ACC) and inﬂammation (IL-1β, TNFα, CD68 and p-JNK), alle-
viating oxidative and ER stress, and decreasing the apoptosis of endothelial cells (TUNEL, BCL-2 and BAX)
induced by HFD and palmitic acid respectively. These ﬁndings suggest that the administration of DJC had
endothelial protective eﬀects against HFD-induced ED, inﬂammation and apoptosis by alleviating lipid de-
position, oxidative and ER stress.
1. Introduction
Obesity is reaching a epidemic proportions, with recent worldwide
ﬁgures estimated at 1.4 billion and rising year-on-year [1]. Individuals
with a central deposition of adipose tissue can experience elevated
cardiovascular morbidity and mortality, and the American Heart As-
sociation has reclassiﬁed obesity as a ‘major, modiﬁable risk factor’ for
coronary heart disease [2].
Endothelium plays a crucial role in maintaining vascular integrity
and function. Continual hyperlipidaemia induced by a high-fat diet
(HFD) can cause vascular endothelial dysfunction (ED) and increase the
vascular permeability, thus leading to a series of pathological changes.
ED is an early biomarker of vascular injury, usually develops through
the loss of normal endothelium-dependent vasodilatation (EDV) re-
sponses to acetylcholine (Ach), and is indicated by the imbalance be-
tween serum nitric oxide (NO) and endothelin-1 (ET-1) levels [3].
Oxidative stress (OS) has been proposed to be a potential pathogenic
mechanism linking obesity and insulin resistance with ED [4].

Overproduction of reactive oxygen species (ROS) disrupts the balance
between oxidant and antioxidant defence systems. The oxidant systems
are composed of NADPH oxidase, xanthine oxidase and lipid oxidation
product malondialdehyde (MDA), meanwhile antioxidant systems in-
clude glutathione peroxidase (GSH-Px), catalase (CAT) and superoxide
dismutase (SOD) [5]. Thus, attenuation of OS is a strategy to deal with
HFD- induced vascular injury.
OS and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress are interconnected.
Misfolded proteins induce the production of reactive oxygen species
ROS; likewise, OS disturbs the ER redox state, thereby disrupting the
correct disulphide bond formation and the proper protein folding [6].
The unfolded protein response (UPR) is induced by activating specia-
lised sensors including inositol-requiring 1α (IRE1α), RNA-dependent
protein kinase-like ER kinase and activating transcription factor 6
(ATF6). As a UPR target gene, glucose-regulated protein 78 (GRP78)
activates the ER stress sensors upon ER stress to adapt to the changing
environment. However, prolonged and/or excess ER stress will even-
tually result in the signiﬁcant expression of C/EBP homologous protein
(CHOP) and thus cause apoptosis, inﬂammation, autophagy and other
pathophysiological processes, including ED [7].
Obesity is known to be associated with elevated circulating non-
esteriﬁed fatty acid levels which cause lipotoxicity and insulin re-
sistance, impair EDV and elevate systemic inﬂammation [8,9]. Inter-
leukin 1β (IL-1β) and tumour necrosis factor α (TNF-α) are two pro-
inﬂammatory cytokines, and they signiﬁcantly increased in obesity-
induced inﬂammation. HFD-induced ED implicates multiple pathologic
processes that vary as the ED progresses. To cope with these processes,
an intervention targeting multiple links is thus required.
Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) has been applied in clinic in
China and some Asian nations for over 2000 years. As indicated in the
theory of TCM, blood is the mother (producer) of qi and qi is the mother
(stimulator) of blood; qi and blood are the main components disturbed
in vascular damage [10]. Conversely, the accumulation of yin means
blood stagnation in microcapillary in the theory of TCM [11].
Danzhi Jiangtang Capsule (DJC) was formulated on the basis of the
TCM theory, and it has been used to treat diabetes accompanied with
vascular complication in clinic for more than 10 years [12]. DJC is
composed
of
Radix
Pseudostellariae,
Radix
Rehmanniae,
Cortex
Moutan, dodder, alisma and leech. Radix Pseudostellariae is known to
invigorate the qi of the spleen and kidney. Radix Rehmanniae can
nourish the yin of the spleen and kidney. Dodder can tonify the kidney
to arrest spontaneous emission. Alisma can clear heat and purge
phlegm. Cortex Moutan and leech can promote qi circulation, in-
vigorate blood circulation, dissolve stagnant blood and resolve kidney
collateral obstruction. Therefore, DJC is eﬃcacious in supplementing
qi, nourishing yin and invigorating blood circulation, and it is known to
downregulate MCP-1 mRNA expression in patients with type 2 diabetes
mellitus (T2DM) subclinical vascular lesions [12].
A meta-analysis showed a statistical decrease in the serum trigly-
ceride (TG), total cholesterol (TC), low density lipoprotein-cholesterol
(LDL-C) and increase in high density lipoprotein-cholesterol (HDL-C)
levels by DJC therapy in comparison with T2DM, thereby indicating the
possible eﬀects of DJC therapy in regulating lipid metabolism [13].
Another study showed that DJC improved the antioxidase activities and
regulated p38MAPK signaling in DM rats [14]. DJC also reduced lipid
deposition in skeletal muscle, regulated ER stress-related IRE1α-JNK
signaling pathway and thus improved skeletal insulin resistance in
obese rats [15]. However, little attention has been given to the eﬀect of
DJC on the lesions of endothelial cells in obese rat models.
In this study, we hypothesized that DJC may improve HFD-induced
ED and inﬂammation via a mechanism that involves antioxidant ac-
tivities and alleviation of ER stress. To test this hypothesis, we eval-
uated the antioxidant and antiinﬂamatory eﬀects of DJC in vivo and in
vitro, also investigated the eﬀects of DJC on expression of ER stress
related molecules such as IRE1α, CHOP and GRP78 to illuminate the
multichannel and multitarget regulating eﬀects of DJC.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Experimental animals and protocols
DJC was purchased from the Pharmaceutical Formulations Centre at
the First Aﬃliated Hospital of Anhui University of Traditional Chinese
Medicine, and it had 1.8 g of eﬀective extract in each capsule. All an-
imal procedures were performed in accordance with the principles
approved by the Animal Ethics Committee of Anhui Medical University.
Forty Eight-week-old male Sprague-Dawley (SD) rats (speciﬁc pa-
thogen-free) were purchased from the Experimental Animal Center of
Anhui Medical University (Anhui, China) and acclimated for 1 week.
The rats were housed in plastic cages (ﬁve rats/cage) at room tem-
perature (22 °C–25 °C) and 35%–60% humidity under a 12:12 h light
and dark cycle. All of the rats were allowed free access to laboratory
chow and water. The rats were randomly divided into four groups:
standard chow diet (SCD), high-fat diet (HFD), HFD with DJC low-dose
treatment group (HFD + DJCL) and HFD with DJC high-dose treatment
group
(HFD + DJCH).
The
rats
in
the
HFD,
HFD + DJCL
and
HFD + DJCH group were given a HFD (containing 55% normal chow,
12% lard, 5% cane sugar, 8% milk powder, 5% peanut, 10% hen eggs,
3% sesame oil, and 2% common salt) ad libitum for three months. Then
the rats in HFD + DJCL and HFD + DJCH groups underwent in-
tragastric administration with DJC (500 and 1000 mg/kg/day) ac-
cording to the literature [15] with a minor modiﬁcation for another two
months respectively. Body weight and food intake were measured once
a week throughout the investigation.
2.2. Serum parameters measurements
Intact thoracic aortas were immediately collected for vascular ten-
sion measurement after ﬁve rats in each group were fasted and anaes-
thetized with 10% chloral hydrate (i.p., 0.35 g/kg body weight). The
remaining rats were killed and the thoracic aortas were used to de-
termine the pathological changes or gene expression. Blood was
sterilely collected through the carotid artery and serum samples were
separated for biochemical analyses, including TG, TC, HDL-C and LDL-C
by colorimetric enzymatic assays in an automatic analyzer (Roche,
cobas 8000, Germany). Serum SOD activity (A001-1), total antioxidant
capacity (T-AOC, A015-1), MDA (A003-1), Free fatty acid (FFA, A042-
1) and NO (A012-1) levels were measured according to the commercial
kit
instructions.

China). Serum IL-1β levels were determined by an ultrasensitive rat IL-

2.3. Isometric tension experiment
Isometric tension experiment was performed as described by Yunxia
Lu et al. to conﬁrm that HFD was responsible for ED and that DJC
showed protective eﬀects on thoracic aorta [16]. Arteries were stimu-
lated with phenylephrine hydrochloride (PE, 10−6 mol/L Aladdin In-
dustrial Corporation, Shanghai, China, Cat No: 61-76-7), followed by
cumulative concentrations of Acetylcholine chloride (Ach, 10−8-10-4
mol/L, Sigma Chemical Company, St. Louis, USA, Cat No: A6625) to
assess the endothelial function. The recorded EDV curves were plotted
as percentages of the contraction values induced by PE.
2.4. Histology, immunohistochemistry and in situ apoptosis assay
The thoracic aortas were ﬁxed in 10% formalin, embedded in par-
aﬃn, sectioned (thickness of 5 μm), stained with haematoxylin and
eosin (H&E), and Masson trichrome [17], respectively. Oil Red O
staining was used to detect the neutral lipids in frozen thoracic aorta

software [18]. The thoracic aorta slides were incubated overnight at
4 °C with rabbit anti-rat CD68 (sc-70761, Santa Cruz, USA). The reac-

(Wuhan Boster Biotechnology, China). Free 3′−OH strand breaks re-
sulting from DNA degradation were detected using the TdT-mediated
dUTP nick-end labeling (TUNEL) technique which was performed ac-
cording to the manusfacturer’s instructions (Roche Molecular Bio-
chemicals, Mannheim, Germany).
2.5. Reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR)
The thoracic aorta was used to analyse the mRNA expression by RT-
PCR. The genes involved in ER stress (e.g. ATF6 and IRE1α), down-
stream eﬀectors (e.g. XBP1, GRP78 and CHOP), carnitine palmitoyl
transferase 1b (CPT1b), acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) and eNOS were
measured.

2.6. Preparation of DJC-medicated serum
Thirty-ﬁve SD rats were divided into normal (n = 15), DJCL
(n = 10), and DJCH (n = 10) groups, and were intragastrically ad-
ministered with distilled water, 1000 mg/kg/day DJC (DJCL) and
2000 mg /kg/day DJC (DJCH), respectively, for 14 days. At the second
day after the last administration, the rats were anaesthetized with 10%
chloral hydrate (i.p., 0.35 g/kg body weight). Blood was sterilely col-
lected through the carotid artery. After settling for 2 h at room tem-
perature, the blood samples were centrifuged at 3000 r/min at room
temperature for 10 min. The samples were stored at −80 °C after being
ﬁltered through a microﬁltrate membrane (0.22 μm), and inactivated at
56 °C for 30 min before the cell experiment [19].

3. Results
3.1. Eﬀects of DJC on obesity and improvement of blood characteristics of
HFD-fed rats
All male SD rats began the experiment with basically similar body
masses. Actual food intake showed no overt diﬀerences among the four
groups (p＞0.05). However, three months of HFD feeding caused sig-
niﬁcantly more body mass, and two months of DJC treatment (500 and
1000 mg/kg/day)
clearly
reduced
body
mass
(p＜0.05),
but
no
diﬀerence was observed between the two treatment groups (Fig. 1). As
shown in Table 2, serum TG, TC and LDL-C levels all increased in the
HFD group, and the HDL-C levels decreased in the HFD group. Two DJC
treatment groups inverted the above changes and exhibited a dose-
dependent eﬀect in a way.
Compared with those of age-matched SCD-fed male rats, the serum
levels of ET-1, FFA, MDA, IL-1β and TNF-α in the HFD-fed male rats
were elevated signiﬁcantly with the reduction of serum NO, SOD and T-
AOC levels (Fig. 2A–H). Compared with those of the HFD group, the
serum levels of ET-1, FFA, MDA and TNF-α decreased signiﬁcantly, and
the serum NO, SOD and T-AOC levels increased signiﬁcantly. Moreover,
serum ET-1, NO, T-AOC, SOD and IL-1β levels exhibited a dose-de-
pendent eﬀect between the two DJC treatment groups (Fig. 2). These
results showed that DJC minimized the ED, inﬂammation and OS and
displayed a dose-dependent eﬀect. As the HFD-fed male rats showed
increased plasma FFA levels, we selected PA as the representative HFD
ingredient to examine the eﬀects of FFA on HUVEC.
3.2. Eﬀects of DJC on pathology, lipid deposition and apoptosis in the
thoracic aorta
H&E staining showed pathological changes, including irregular
thickening of the thoracic aortic wall as well as disorders and fractures
of elastic ﬁbres in the HFD-fed rats (Fig. 3). Oil Red-O staining con-
ﬁrmed that more neutral lipids were deposited on the vascular walls of

HFD + DJCL and HFD + DJCH groups displayed improvements in pa-

3.5. Eﬀect of DJC-medicated medium on intracellular ROS levels in HUVEC
treated with PA
Palmitic acid is known to induce OS [20]. The fact that DJC in the
vivo experiment decreased MDA and increased the T-AOC and SOD
levels in serum, thus alleviating OS (Fig. 2), prompted us to investigate
the eﬀect of DJC-medicated serum on intracellular ROS production in
PA-induced HUVEC. The DJC-medicated serum was used to represent
the two diﬀerent DJC doses. The results showed that ROS generation
was signiﬁcantly increased by PA treatment, whereas the DJC-medi-
cated serum decreased the ROS levels in diﬀerent degrees in compar-
ison with the PA treatment and the positive control (Rosup) (Fig. 6).
3.6. Eﬀect of DJC-medicated medium on intracellular CHOP distribution
and expression in HUVEC treated with PA
As the proapoptotic transcription factor CHOP is a typical marker of
ER stress [21], immunoﬂuorescence assay was performed to detect the
expression and distribution of CHOP in HUVEC, with the ﬂuorescent
dye DAPI labelling the nucleus. Our results showed that CHOP was
expressed and mainly localised in the cytoplasm induced by PA or TM,
and that DJC-medicated serum decreased the protein expression of
CHOP in PA-treated HUVEC (Fig. 7).
3.7. Eﬀect of DJC-medicated serum on gene expression in HUVEC treated
with PA
The mechanisms of DJC-medicated serum on OS and ER stress were
detected in the PA-treated HUVEC. TM and PBA were used as the ER
stress inducer and inhibitor, respectively. PA decreased the protein
expressions of p-eNOS and SIRT1, and induced the protein expression of
IRE1α, GRP78 and CHOP. The DJC-medicated serum could revert the
protein expression of p-eNOS, SIRT1, IRE1α, GRP78 and CHOP, and
exhibited a dose-dependent eﬀect (Figs. 8A and B). When HUVEC were
treated with H2O2 to induce OS, the protein expression of p-eNOS and
SIRT1 were decreased, whereas the DJC-medicated serum increased
their expression (Fig. 8C and D). To conﬁrm the eﬀect of alleviating ER
stress by the DJC-medicated serum, the HUVEC were directly treated
with TM. Again, the result showed that the DJC-medicated serum de-
creased the protein expression of IRE1α, GRP78 and CHOP elevated by
TM treatment (Fig. 8E and F). In summary, the results shown in
Fig. 8C–F veriﬁed that PA could induce the occurrence of OS and ER
stress, and that the DJC-medicated serum alleviated OS and ER stress.
4. Discussion
The entire DJC prescription can supplement qi and nourish yin,
invigorate blood circulation and dissolve stagnant blood, thus achieving
the eﬃcacy of balancing yin and yang. The main ﬁndings of the present
study revealed that treatment with DJC decreased body mass and serum
lipid indices, attenuated the HFD-induced vascular inﬂammation, im-
proved EDV and prevented apoptosis and lipid deposition in the en-
dothelium, which seemed to be related to the attenuation of OS and ER
stress and thus beneﬁcial to the endothelial cells. This work is the ﬁrst
complete study to compare the eﬀects of diﬀerent doses of DJC on
biochemical, morphological and functional alterations in the thoracic
aorta of HFD-fed animal models and in PA - treated HUVEC.
As many basic and clinical studies have been conducted on DJC, and
DJC has no any reported toxicity until now, so the SCD + DJCL,
SCD + DJCH and the positive drug treatment groups weren’t included
in our animal study. DJC had the eﬀect of reducing the body mass and
serum TG, TC, LDL-C and FFA levels induced by HFD (Table 2). It also
reduced lipid deposition in the thoracic aorta (Fig. 3, Oil Red O
staining), decreased the ACC expression and increased the CPT1b ex-
pression. These results indicated that DJC has the lipid-lowering ac-
tivities, which were conﬁrmed in newly diagnosed T2DM treated with
DJCs [12,13], so we speculate that DJC may have an eﬀect on adipo-
genesis and energy expenditure, but this will be demonstrated in future.
Hyperlipidaemia is known to impair endothelial function in ex-
perimental animals and humans [22,23]. Endothelium-derived NO is
the most important modulator of the vascular tone in the rat aorta and
ET-1 is a typical vasoconstrictor. The opposite changes in NO and ET-1
levels in the serum of the HFD and HFD + DJC rats indicated the ex-
istence of ED and improvement by DJC treatment in vivo (Fig. 2). The
DJC treatment increased the expression of p-eNOS in the thoracic aorta
(Fig. 5E–F) and the HUVEC (Fig. 8A–D), and it was partly contributed to
the increased NO levels in serum.
Lipid-induced inﬂammation contributes to the damage and repair of
endothelial cell [24] and has been recognised as a target for the
treatment of HFD-induced vascular injury. Pharmacological therapy
targeting the various components in this series of events is considered a
strategy for coping with HFD-induced vascular injury. Our results
showed that DJC treatment decreased the serum IL-1β and TNF-α levels
and reduced the inﬁltration of CD68-positive cells and p-JNK expres-
sion in the thoracic aorta. Thus, DJC exhibited multi anti-inﬂammatory
eﬀects on obesity-induced inﬂammation.
Lipid induces OS. Modern pharmacology studies found that Radix
Pseudostellariae and Moutan bark could increase SOD and decrease
MDA levels to inhibit OS [25,26]. Zheng et al. reported that DJC ef-
fectively ameliorated OS in type 1 diabetic rats and caused related
changes in T-AOC, SOD activity and MDA content in plasma and pan-
creas [27]. DJC also reversed the advanced glucosylation end products
(AGEs)-induced accumulation of ROS and NADPH oxidase activity, thus
conﬁrming its antioxidant activities [28]. Thus we speculated that DJC
showed the eﬀect of decreasing lipid-induced OS in HFD animals. As-
suredly our study conﬁrmed that DJC decreased the serum MDA con-
tent and increased T-AOC and SOD activities, thereby ameliorating OS
in vivo.
Sirtuin (SIRT1) is a potential mediator of oxidative pathway.
Antioxidant N-acetylcysteine (NAC) attenuated SIRT1 repression, in-
creased SIRT1 mRNA levels and decreased SIRT1 protein degradation in
Antimony-treated cells [29]. The DJC-medicated serum also decreased
the ROS levels and increased SIRT1 expression in PA-treated and H2O2-
treated HUVEC, respectively (Figs. 6 and 8). Thus, DJC actually ex-
hibited anti-oxidative activities by increasing SIRT1 protein expression
in vivo and in vitro, which could be attributed to ﬂavonoids and other
ingredients in Radix Pseudostellariae and Moutan bark. However, this
speculation requires more experiments to conﬁrm it.
ER stress is connected with OS. Therefore, when OS happens, ER
stress also occurs subsequently and they inﬂuence each other. The in-
tervention eﬀect of 470 mg/kg/d DJC could alleviate the IRE1α-JNK
signaling pathway in the skeletal muscle of obese rats [15]. We de-
monstrated that DJC treatment decreased the mRNA and protein ex-
pressions of IRE1α, GRP78 and CHOP in the thoracic aorta (Fig. 5A–D).

The DJC-medicated serum decreased the protein expression of IRE1α,
GRP78 and CHOP in PA-treated and TM-treated HUVEC, respectively.
Thus, DJC did alleviate ER stress in endothelial cells induced by HFD
feeding and PA treatment.
Activated CHOP induced apoptosis, consistent with the decreased
BCL-2 and increased BAX expression. The result of the TUNEL assay
indicated that the apoptosis of the endothelial cells in the thoracic aorta
was induced by HFD, and that DJC treatment decreased the apoptosis of
the endothelial cells in the thoracic aorta. Similarly, the DJC-medicated
serum decreased the distribution and protein expression of BAX and
CHOP in PA-treated HUVEC (Fig. 7).Polysaccharide isolated from
dodder seeds is known to decrease the apoptosis of cardiomyocytes
through the mitochondrial apoptosis pathway [30]. Therefore, dodder
seeds included in DJC could mediate anti-apoptotic eﬀect of DJC in the
HFD-induced thoracic aorta and PA-treated endothelial cells.
Medicinal leech has been widely used as a TCM in cardiovascular
diseases, but its pharmaceutical eﬀect is not fully uncovered. Leech
extract signiﬁcantly reduced atherosclerotic lesions and the number of
macrophage in or around the atherosclerosis plaque in aortic root in
ApoE−/−mice [31].Leech was also included in DJC, and as the one and
only animal component, the improvement of ED (Fig. 4) and the de-
crease in macrophages (CD68-positive cells) in the thoracic aorta by
DJC (Fig. 3) could be related with the leech ingredient in DJC. This
supposition should be conﬁrmed further.
In conclusion, DJC has lipid-lowering, anti-inﬂammatory, and en-
dothelial-protection activities by decreasing OS and ER stress.
